_source.displaydescription:
This Caitya is located to the west of Karuṇāmaya Mandira (BUN0001) and is part of a group of another four caityas and a dharmadhātu maṇḍala, all of which are aligned in a north-south direction. The area surrounding the Caitya is paved with black flagstones and has been encroached upon by some of the building materials for the reconstruction of the Karuṇāmaya Mandira.

The base structure of the Caitya is made from brick and plastered with cement mortar, however, the dome and finial are made of stone. Four Buddha statues have been placed in the niches that face each of the four cardinal directions.

The Caitya was constructed in 1964. An umbrella is placed on top of the Caitya on the full moon day of Āśvina, and its anniversary worship takes place on the full moon day of Vaiśākha.

_source.displaydescription: Cola Nani is located at the northern end of Bungamati. It consists of one Gaṇeśa shrine and three caityas. The shrine was built around 1973; people brought wood from the nearby forest for its construction. Before this, the Gaṇeśa shrine stood in an open space. Leaning against the back wall, Gaṇeśa's house is supported by eight plain columns and has a hip roof covered in tiles (which local residents call Chinese tiles). The Nani is also known as Gubhāḥkhyaḥ Nani due to the fact that Gubhāḥjus and Vajrācāryas live in its vicinity. Local residents say that Bandhudatta Ācārya helped King Narendradeva and Lalita Jyāpu to bring the Red Matsyendranātha to the Kathmandu Valley, and that he lived in this Nani. The Vajrācāryas living in this area therefore believe that they are the descendants of Bandhudatta.

_source.displaydescription:
Narasiṃha Mandira was built by Purandara Siṃha, a mahāpātra of Lalitpur in NS 710 (1590 CE) in memory of his elder brother Narasiṃha Deva. It is one of the few early śikhara towers in the Valley. Although Śaiva mortuary temples are found in many places, this is said to be the first mortuary temple with a Vaiṣṇava image (Tiwari 2013, 113). Two stone lions guard the temple and two guarding deities are installed on the top plinth. The left deity is a four-handed Garuḍa using two hands to pray and the others to hold a flower and a water vessel. The deity sitting on the right-hand side is holding a cakra (wheel), aṅkuśa (hook), gadā and pāśa (noose). Inside the sanctum, an eight-handed stone image of Narasiṃha, the fourth incarnation of Viṣṇu, stands on a pedestal holding khaḍga, cakra, vajra and gadā with his right hands and śaṅkha, pāśa, padma and aṅkuśa with his left hands. Garuḍa sits to his left and Lakṣmī is located to his right. Unlike other commonly found Narasiṃha images, this Narasiṃha is standing but is not pictured tearing apart Hiraṇyakaśipu's abdomen. 

The temple sits on two lower plinths and an upper plinth with porches extending in all four directions. The sanctum tapers upwards towards the śikhara. Located on the ground floor, the main sanctum can be accessed from the east side by a series of steps. Stone pillars rest on either side of the porch, though the columns attached to the walls of the sanctum are made of timber. The lintel beam is also made from timber and has layers of brick cornice above it. Four doorways can be found on each of the sanctum's walls, but the main entrance is on the eastern side. Four porches have been built to form turrets above the sanctum, and are attached to the main śikhara tower. These turrets have small openings on three of their side walls, as well as terracotta toraṇa capped by decorative brick work and a stone finial. Their walls have been plastered with lime. The main brick tower is at the centre and contains seven bands known as saptaratha. The topmost crown of the śikhara is embellished with layers of floral patterned cornices and an āmalaka plastered with lime. The pinnacle is made from stone.

_source.displaydescription: Nāsaḥ Phalcā is a single-storey Phalcā situated in Cyāsal. It stands on the western edge of the route which leads from from Kvaylāchi (south) to the outskirts of Cyāsal (north), and its rear wall is attached to the Nāsaḥ Capāḥ. From the Phalcā, one enters into an office that is located inside but otherwise disconnected from the building of the Capāḥ, which is dedicated to Nāsaḥdhyaḥ, the god of music and dance. The first floor of the Capāḥ is located above Nāsaḥ Phalcā and is used for Hari bhajan. It was reconstructed in 2018 after being dismantled and rebuilt in 1992. None of the historic elements were preserved. The structure now has a cement roof with modern columns. Its associated groups are the Nāsaḥ Guṭhī, the Cyāsaḥ Maṃkā Khalaḥ and the Yanyā Guthi of Byañjankārs of Nhukaṃchẽnani (Mahārānī Cukaḥ).

_source.displaydescription:
Āratī Chẽ, a ceremonial rest house (capāḥ), is closely related to Karuṇāmaya Mandira (BUN0001) and located to the temple's north-west. The building's name translates as "oil lamp house" meaning "the building where oil lamps are prepared".

According to local informants, the original Āratī Chẽ collapsed in the 1934 earthquake and was not reconstructed until 2018. A photo taken in 1968 (published in Bungmati 1968: A Survey by Danish Architect Students, page 21) shows the building site to be empty. The 2018 reconstruction was financed by the Lalitpur Municipality and represents a hybrid structure combining traditional and modern styles and building techniques. The walls have been constructed using regular brick and are painted with surkhi (brick dust and lime mortar). Horizontal and vertical timber bands have been inserted at regular intervals as seismic strengthening devices, something that is not a traditionally found in this type of building. A concrete slab supports the open terrace. The building's main facade (which faces south) has been built in a traditional configuration whereas the facades facing west and north remain unfinished and lack the traditional overhanging roofs.

Oil lamps (āratī) are prepared at Aratī Chẽ for ceremonial use at the Karuṇāmaya temple. The deity Buṅgadyaḥ (also known as Karuṇāmaya) is worshipped four times a day: in the early morning, at noon, in the evening and in the middle of the night. Oil lamps are offered to the deity at the end of each worship (see Locke 1985, 238 for more details).

The Aratī Chẽ guṭhī is managed by a Śākya family, one of the 31 priest families of Karuṇāmaya Mandira. This family prepares the oil lamps and brings them to the temple. In the time between the building's destruction in 1934 and its reconstruction in 2018, the family prepared the oil lamps in their house.

_source.displaydescription:
Buṅga Bahī, also known as Prathampura Mahāvihāra, is located at the northwestern end of Buṅgamatī. The monument can be reached from the northern gate of the Karuṇāmaya Mandira (BUN0001). This bahī is in Lalitpur but is not counted among the major bahīs of the district. It is named after Buṅgamatī, but is also referred to as Prathamapura Mahāvihāra, meaning the first bahī of the area. It is under the ownership of local Śākyas. These people write their last name as Brahmācārya Bhikṣu.

The bahī has four entrances, one at each of its four sides, but the eastern one forms the main entrance. The bahī's hip roof is supported by plain struts, whilst the first floor is held up by double-layered pillars. As is often the case with bahī,  one can find a phucā atop its roof. However, the śivaliṅga-shaped finial sets this bahī apart from others; these structures generally have a caitya-shaped finial. A veranda surrounds the first floor of the bahī complex. Inside, an L-shaped staircase leads up to the first floor.

The sanctum of the bahī is on the first floor of the western building and houses an east-facing statue of Akṣobhya. Two stone lions and two metal flags flank the entrance of the sanctum. Carved panels depicting a Gandharva, a female figure and a water vessel have been fixed on either side of the entrance.  A śivaliṅga-shaped aśoka caitya stands in the courtyard.

No historical record could be found with which to date the bahī. However, a local folk tale tells that Matsyendranātha was brought to the Valley and requested to live in Bungmati. However, he replied that he did not want to dwell in a place without a bahī. As a result, this bahī was constructed and the deity accepted the request to live here. According to the bahī members, this bahī was established by Dhyānacandra Miśra. Three merchant brothers from Patan, Dharmaśrī Miśra, Jñānaśrī Miśra and Dhyānacandra Miśra, spent the money they had earned through Tibetean trade to establish three bahīs. These are known as Kvanti Bahī, I Bahī and the present bahī. However, no historical record is available to verify this claim. The only inscriptions found in the bahī complex stem from the late Malla period.

The bahī suffered from multiple earthquakes and has undergone reconstruction multiple times. This took place most recently in 2005 and was carried out by the Department of Archeology in Nepal.

The main worship rituals that take place are the annual ritual worship of the caitya, a Vasundharā worship, a Mahākāla worship, and a srāddha (a ritual performed in honour of dead relatives) for Dhyānacandra Miśra. A guṭhī endowed with 45 ropanī of land in Bungmati and Sunaguthi was established to run the social and religious activities of the bahī (Locke 1985, 223). However, some of the guṭhī's lands have been privatised, and even the tenant farmers working the other lands no longer give the bahī's share to the guṭhī. The saṅgha-members of the bahī therefore rely on the collection of donations in order to fund these activities.

_source.displaydescription: Two dharmadhātujinālaya caityas, commonly referred to as chaturamukha caitya (i.e a caitya which has four faces) and a dharmadhātu maṇḍala are located on the western side of the main road at Hitipusaḥ Jaḥrũ, Dampāchẽ, Sunāguthi. Four Buddha images sit on top of the upward opening lotus blossoms above a single layer of petals. These blossoms are supported by a lion throne positioned on top of a square pedestal which in turn sits upon the square plinth. A drum, a dome and a finial have been placed above the four Buddha images. The caityas are 200 cm in height. An octagonal shaped dharmadhātu maṇḍala (80 cm in height) lies to their west.

Kani Bāhāḥ is a branch of Oku Bāhāḥ (Rudravarṇa Mahāvihāra, LAL2260) and was established in 1702 (NS 822) by Devarāja Śākya. It is located at the southeast corner of Lalitpur city, on the way to Sincāhiti from Oku Bāhāḥ. This Bāhāḥ is on the fringe of the city, at the crossroad of the roads from Prayag Pokhari to Gwarko and Satdobato. It can be accessed via a carved door on the northern side of the complex. The front facade of the main door has changed and shops have been built up around it. Two doors have also been added on either side of it.

The main door is accentuated by two small blind windows and carvings of deities on either side of it. Entering the door via a vestibule, one finds a colonnaded space (phalcā) on the second bay, as well as images of Gaṇeśa, Mahākāla and Hanumān to the left, on the eastern wall, and an image of Bhīmasena to the right, on the western wall. The Phalcā has three bays and a pair of columns (jvaḥthā̃). The main courtyard is surrounded by a plinth, measures 8.85m x 8.85m, and is 45cm below the level of the Phalcā. 

The main sanctum building is a three-storey structure built on the southern wing of the courtyard. It has a richly carved central main door on the ground floor that is flanked by two small windows with circular lattice work on either side. The upper floor is distinguished by a band of carved timber cornice that is typical to Newar architecture. On the first floor, one can find a pasukā jhyāh with two aedicules on either side. The second floor is mainly occupied by a central slanting projected window known as gā jhyāḥ. The sanctum building has two exit doors on the ground floor; the eastern door leads to an open space to the south, while the western one is the entrance to a residential building. There are two lattice windows on the first floor and one single window on the second floor. The roof is covered with jhiṅgati tiles and has a stūpa finial on its ridge. The building now stands in the shadow of a newly constructed five-storey building behind it, i.e. to its south.

The courtyard is well paved with high quality teliyā tiles. It contains a Durgatipariśodhana caitya (220cm high), a statue of some donors and a dharmadhātu maṇḍala (80cm high). These are all lined up in front of the main sanctum building.

The north-facing god house of the Bāhāḥ has three storeys, though it was seriously affected by the 2015 earthquake. It can be found at the southern side of the courtyard. Its worn tiled-roof is damaged in some parts, and vegetation is growing on and through it. Although the roof is dilapidated, it is still topped by a caitya-shaped pinnacle.

According to Bāhāḥ members, Lalitpur Metropolitan City provided 28 Lakh Rupees for the reconstruction of the monastery.
_source.displayname: Kani Bāhāḥ at Oku Bāhāḥ (1702 CE) || कनि बाहाः ॥ LAL2240
